lesson.title: What Rolle's Theorem Needs to Work
lesson.summary: Rolle's Theorem needs all three of its conditions at once, continuity, differentiability, and equal endpoint values, and losing even one, right at the point where the flat spot would have to be, can erase the guarantee entirely.
lesson.body:
Rolle's Theorem carries three requirements: f continuous on [a,b], f differentiable on (a,b), and f(a) = f(b). The first two are inherited directly from the Mean Value Theorem, for exactly the same reasons discussed with the Mean Value Theorem's conditions: continuity rules out jumps and holes, and differentiability on the open interval guarantees an actual tangent line, and hence a derivative, to work with at every interior point. The third condition, equal endpoint values, is what turns the Mean Value Theorem's general guaranteed point into specifically a horizontal tangent guarantee. Drop any one of the three and the flat spot conclusion can no longer be relied on.

Consider f(x) = |x - 2| on the interval [1,3]. Check the endpoint values first: f(1) = |1-2| = 1, and f(3) = |3-2| = 1, so f(1) = f(3) = 1, and the equal endpoints condition holds. f is also continuous on all of [1,3], since absolute value functions are continuous everywhere. But f is not differentiable at x = 2, which sits right in the interior of (1,3): the graph has a sharp corner there, with slope -1 immediately to the left and slope +1 immediately to the right, and no tangent line at the corner itself. If Rolle's Theorem applied, some c in (1,3) would have f'(c) = 0. But f'(x) equals -1 for every x less than 2 and +1 for every x greater than 2, and it is simply undefined at the one point, x = 2, where a horizontal tangent might have appeared. No c in (1,3) has f'(c) = 0, so the conclusion fails, entirely because differentiability broke down at one interior point.

It is worth noticing what this example has in common with the earlier Rolle's Theorem worked example, f(x) = x^2 - 4x + 3 on [1,3], where the guaranteed flat spot landed exactly at x = 2, the vertex of the parabola. Here, x = 2 is again the natural location where a flat spot would have to occur, since it sits symmetrically between the two points of equal height at x = 1 and x = 3. But instead of a smooth minimum with a well defined horizontal tangent, the graph has a corner at x = 2, and the derivative simply does not exist there. Rolle's Theorem does not offer a fallback plan for a missing derivative; it either finds a genuine horizontal tangent somewhere in the open interval, or, if differentiability fails at the one place it was needed, the guarantee is gone.

The practical lesson is to check all three conditions before invoking Rolle's Theorem, not just the equal endpoints condition, which is often the most visually obvious one. A function can look symmetric and well behaved and still hide a single corner or jump that quietly removes the guarantee.
